newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Protests and promises in Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: Protests and promises in Kabila's Congo.

text.p: Beating girls in mini-skirts is not official government policy in Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo.
A witch-hunt by soldiers who stripped girls in short skirts or tight trousers had no official backing, Kabila's administration said in a weekend statement read on state radio and televion.
The announcement could be seen as a sign of sensitivity to public opinion from a man hailed by some as a liberator, denounced by others as a closet dictator.
Or was it a simple sop to the people of a city once one of Africa's liveliest and free-wheeling capitals?

"This form of dress is certainly reprehensible but the manner in which the operation was conducted did not please the public," state radio and television said, quoting a statement from Kabila's first cabinet meeting.
Kabila's forces ousted veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko on May 17 after a seven-month civil war. His first moves since taking office as president on Thursday have been firm and uncompromising.

He has banned all political activity and taken sweeping powers. Elections are promised by April 1999 -- but on his terms -- and he has turned his back on the opposition which challenged Mobutu from within.
Within days of his arrival in the capital, students supporting veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, an implacable foe of Mobutu, took to the streets to denounce him.
At Kabila's inauguration dissident sections of the crowd chanted their support for Tshisekedi and for immediate democracy.
Opposition militants say Kabila is a pawn in the hands of neighbouring Rwanda's Tutsi leadership. They denounce the presence of Rwandans among his forces and demand that they return home.
Despite the considerable support that Tshisekedi enjoys in the teeming capital, there are signs that a growing number of people want to see what Kabila, 57, has to offer.
Kabila's Congo is Africa's third largest and potentially one of its richest nations. It has a wealth of mineral resources, rich farmland and huge hydroelectric potential.
Three decades of official corruption and administrative chaos under Mobutu have left it virtually bankrupt.
Kabila won enthusiastic applause at his inauguration when he said unemployment must be eliminated. He spoke of mining and agro-industrial development.
His government on Friday announced plans to rebuild roads and hospitals, boost farm training and build a national oil supply pipeline.

"Tshisekedi was good in the past but we should give Kabila a chance," says Jean Kingassam, 65, a taxi driver and father of 12 from Tshisekedi's home region of Kasai. "It's stable. The children go to school. There is security," he adds.

"There are those who want to march but most of us want to study," Lambert Mouamba, 23, a civil aviation student at the Higher Institute of Applied Technology ISTA, a traditional hotbed of political protest, said on Friday. Others nodded their approval.
On the bustling sidewalk near Victory Square, a staunch Tshisekedi stronghold, animated groups gathered in the wake of the latest banned opposition march.
"We would like to march but we can't. With the soldiers there, we're afraid," confides Jean-Marie Loemi, 20.

On Friday, the soldiers tracked the marchers all the way to Tshsisekedi's street -- and did not intervene. "That shows a certain flexibility on our part," Information Minister Raphael Ghenda said afterwards, adding this would not necessarily last.
Kabila has won the support of South Africa's Nelson Mandela and the United States for his view that he cannot rush into elections.
His Alliance has signed at least one mining contract and says it will review those signed under Mobutu.
But he and his administration, which has admitted that the state coffers are virtually empty, have yet to spell out their plans in detail and say precisely how they plan to fund them.
